anchors.fact: At twenty-one, in 1979, he asked Ray at the Tiki-Ti "What's in this drink?" and, "no matter what the drink", heard "Rum and fruit juice", "everywhere I went" (Proper p. 258). (F2)
anchors.meaning: An answer that is true and explains nothing. *Our reading:* it wasn't even a lie.
anchors.speaksTo: the one true thing: can't rest inside an answer that explains nothing; fear: entrapment, stuck with an answer they can't get behind

anchors.fact: Ray Buhen had worked at the original Don the Beachcomber; Beach had told him (not "his staff") never to reveal trade secrets, lest competing tiki bars adopt them, and he "was only acting on ingrained instincts" (Proper pp. 258–259). (F3)
anchors.meaning: Nobody was hiding anything from him in particular. The answer was a habit, not a villain.

anchors.fact: Many recipes, "including the Zombie", were lost by the time Berry started asking (Proper p. 259); in 1998 he put it in print that nobody seemed to know what went into the Zombie (Oxford pdf 260, Curtis quoting him). (F3, F8)
anchors.meaning: The one question that stayed open.
anchors.speaksTo: hidden: how long it's been. Guard: paraphrase the 1998 line (*The First Guess*); never "he asked about the Zombie in 1979" (C2); never "the one nobody could explain" or "the one he still couldn't answer" (many were lost; he decoded many others, pdf 260; A8, my shorthand struck)

anchors.fact: By day he wrote film trailers and poster copy (Proper p. 259), later "his day job as a screenwriter" (Oxford pdf 259); through the 1980s, "I was working completely in isolation" (Proper p. 259). (F4, F5)
anchors.meaning: Held alongside an ordinary life, for years, without telling anyone.
anchors.speaksTo: hidden: they've stopped mentioning it. Guard: one clause, "a day job in films"; no Home Alone; the guest is never called lonely

anchors.fact: He interviewed retired bartenders, and their children where the bartender was gone; many recipes were "written in code" (Oxford pdf 259); off-hours he read microfilm in libraries and hunted former Beachcomber and Trader Vic barmen (Proper pp. 260–261). (F6, F7)
anchors.meaning: Evidence from the people who made the drinks, not anyone's say-so.
anchors.speaksTo: goal: understanding; trusts evidence. Guard: the code gets one clause, no secret-recipe romance

anchors.fact: Ted Haigh, a "fellow cocktail historian" (Oxford pdf 259; not "friend", A16), "Gregarious and bombastic", "was the opposite of Berry" (Proper p. 259). Alone Berry got "rum and fruit juice"; with Haigh "he walked away with a recipe"; "The first Don the Beachcomber recipes I got were because of Ted" (p. 260). They met in the 1990s (Oxford pdf 259). (H1, H2, H4)
anchors.meaning: The door opened when he took the question to the person least like him.
anchors.speaksTo: the proposal (Wren's y5 candidate). Guard: Beachcomber recipes in general, **never the Zombie**; no Corpse Reviver, "skeleton key" or "Dr. Cocktail"

anchors.fact: Berry said it took "ten years and three books" to nail down the Zombie's origins (Oxford pdf 260). (F9)
anchors.meaning: The years were his own count, and he didn't stop.
anchors.speaksTo: hidden: how long it's been. Guard: always "he said"; no arithmetic from 1998

anchors.fact: In *Sippin' Safari* (2007) he revealed "an early recipe" from a self-published 1950 three-ring-binder cookbook whose author thanked Don the Beachcomber for his "generous assistance"; he later turned up a 1934 Zombie Punch and a 1956 recipe in *Cabaret* (Oxford pdf 260). (F10, F11)
anchors.meaning: Pieces, each on paper, none the whole answer yet.
anchors.speaksTo: evidence wins, not charm. Guard: the binder is never "the original" (C1)

anchors.fact: In the ZOMBIE entry he signed himself, Berry writes that the original formula Beach "took to his grave" was found by him in 2006 in the notebook of former Beachcomber's headwaiter Richard Santiago (Oxford pdf 2229). (F12)
anchors.speaksTo: the one true thing: they love the day they know. Guard: "what he calls the original"; no order against the binder (C1); no "as he tells it" frame (*Worth the Trip* y2)

anchors.fact: He printed the whole recipe in that entry, every part named and measured, including "Don's Mix", spelled out as two parts grapefruit to one part cinnamon syrup (Oxford pdf 2229); Regan reprints it from Berry's site (Joy pdf 409). Codex p. 179: Donn's Mix No. 1 is "a classic tiki syrup made with grapefruit juice and cinnamon syrup". (F14, F19)
anchors.meaning: Handed over whole, so nobody has to take it on trust.
anchors.speaksTo: gift: hand over the whole answer, plainly. Guard: never "the old recipes hid" grapefruit and cinnamon (A12); our glass is *a* Zombie, not *the* (A10)

anchors.fact: Seven books "featuring definitive recipes" (Oxford pdf 259); Smuggler's Cove and Three Dots and a Dash "owed a debt to Berry" and were "near-instant successes" (never "hugely", A6), and Three Dots is named after a lost tiki drink whose recipe he uncovered (Proper p. 262); he "made a convincing case" that tiki drinks were among the original craft cocktails (Oxford pdf 259). (F1, F17, F18)
anchors.meaning: Something everyone had written off is seen properly again.
anchors.speaksTo: gift: things written off get seen properly. Guard: no "Eighty percent", no "shamed" **Not in the reading since 2026-10-06** (Q054 cut y2's last sentence); dossier only.

anchors.fact: Craft cocktail people "didn't want to touch tiki with a ten-foot pole" (Proper p. 257); "the mavens… paid him little heed" for many years (p. 261). (F16)
anchors.meaning: Standing didn't move him. The evidence did, in the end.
anchors.speaksTo: Sage: authority that can't explain itself. Guard: no villains, no grievance

anchors.fact: The glass: the parts of the Zombie as Berry printed it (Oxford pdf 2229), shaken and poured over crushed ice as the Codex's own Zombie is (Codex p. 127), with Tomás's proportions.
anchors.meaning: Every part named, in the glass. The proportions and the shake are ours.
anchors.speaksTo: the drink as proof. Guard: never "Beach's recipe", "his recipe" or "the notebook's recipe" for our glass

anchors.fact: Falernum: "recipes vary"; rum, sugar and lime, with cloves, ginger and nutmeg; "Almonds are sometimes added" (Oxford pdf 761). Berry went "gathering ferns and Falernum recipes" from the old barmen (Proper p. 261). (F20)
anchors.meaning: A bought bottle is the one part you'd take on trust. Ours is made at home, with every part known. *Our riff.*
anchors.speaksTo: gift: nothing taken on trust. Veto: bought falernum counts as nuts

anchors.fact: "6 drops Pernod" (Oxford pdf 2229; Joy pdf 409). Regan lists Pernod among the absinthe *substitutes* (Joy pdf 64) and treats Pernod and absinthe as two bottles (Joy pdf 395); the Codex's own Zombie uses "Pernod Absinthe" (p. 127), which the Codex counts among its absinthe bottlings (p. 34). (C5)
anchors.speaksTo: Guard: if kept, "Pernod (the anise liqueur)", never "absinthe" (*Rosetta*'s bottle)

cocktail.closingLine: Write everything that's in the falernum on its bottle. Then ask your oldest question out loud.
cocktail.glassware: a tall Zombie glass, filled with crushed ice
method: **The falernum (10 minutes, then a day; makes about 375 ml, enough for about 20 drinks).** With a vegetable peeler, take the green zest off 4 limes, leaving the white pith behind. Put the zest and 12 whole cloves in a clean lidded container with 150 ml of the gold Jamaican rum, and leave it at room temperature for 24 hours. Strain it. In a small pan, warm 200 g of sugar with 100 ml of water, stirring, just until the sugar dissolves, then let it cool. Stir the syrup into the strained rum and pour it into a clean bottle. Write everything that went in on the bottle. It keeps in the fridge for a few months.

**The cinnamon syrup (5 minutes, then 30 minutes off the heat).** Warm 200 g of sugar in 200 ml of water with 3 cinnamon sticks, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then let it simmer for 2 minutes. Take it off the heat and leave it for 30 minutes, then strain. It keeps in the fridge for about two weeks.
Fill the tall glass with crushed ice so it chills while you mix.
Put everything except the mint in a shaker. The grapefruit juice and the cinnamon syrup go in separately: together they're "Don's Mix", two parts grapefruit to one of cinnamon.
Fill the shaker with ice cubes, close it and shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Strain over the crushed ice, and top the glass up with more crushed ice.
Slap the mint sprig once between your palms to wake its scent, then stand it in the ice.
cocktail.name: Show Your Working

recipe.note: the first of the three rums Berry printed

recipe.item: Lemon Hart 151 Demerara rum (75.5%), recommended, or any Demerara (Guyanese) overproof rum of about 70-75%
recipe.note: the third, named in the recipe Berry printed; very strong

recipe.item: falernum, made at home: a lime and clove syrup with rum in it, as they make it in Barbados, but with no almond, no nutmeg and no ginger
recipe.note: a bought falernum may hold almond or nutmeg, so this one is made where you can see what goes in

cocktail.tagline: You'll wait years for the real answer. Then you give it away.

reading.epigraph: Once, if you asked what was in drinks like this, you'd hear: rum and fruit juice.
whoYouAre: Years ago, someone gave you an answer that was perfectly true and told you nothing. You nodded, and kept the question. It has come along ever since, at the back of an ordinary week, and now and then another piece falls into place. Nobody would guess that one of your questions is older than some of your friendships.

You've stopped mentioning it, because people expect a question to be settled or dropped by now. Some take you for a know-it-all. It's nearly the opposite: you can't rest inside something you aren't allowed to understand. What frightens you is being stuck for good with an answer you can't get behind. And once you do understand, you lay all of it out, plainly, so nobody else has to take it on trust. People get the whole answer from you, free, and every year it cost you was worth it.
yours: In 1979, at twenty-one, Jeff Berry started going to tiki bars on his own. At the Tiki-Ti on Sunset Boulevard he asked the old barman, Ray Buhen: "What's in this drink?" Whatever the drink, Ray gave the same reply: "Rum and fruit juice." Berry heard it in bar after bar. Ray wasn't being difficult: he had once worked for Donn Beach, who created the Zombie at his Hollywood bar, and Beach had told him never to give away the bar's trade secrets, in case rival bars copied them. So by the time Berry started asking, many of the old tiki recipes, the Zombie's among them, had become a mystery.

Berry had a day job in films. His off-hours went on the question. He read microfilm in libraries, tracked down retired barmen, and their children when the barmen were gone, and learned to read recipes written in code. In 1998 he put it in print that the Zombie's recipe was still unknown. Getting to the bottom of the Zombie took ten years and three books, he said. He found an early recipe in a self-published cookbook from 1950, and in a former headwaiter's notebook, what he calls the original. And he printed a Zombie with every part named.

The answer that kept Berry going, I like to think, wasn't a no. He could have lived with a no. It was "rum and fruit juice": polite, true, and empty. You've been handed that answer too, more than once. A shrug doesn't end a question for you. It starts one. And his narrowed the way yours do, from every drink on the menu down to one: the Zombie, and then he stayed with it for years, beside an ordinary job, until he could write the whole thing down.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Zombie, the first famous tiki drink and still one of the great ones. Every part Berry printed is in it, and your recipe names each one. Two of them, grapefruit and cinnamon, travel under one old name, Don's Mix, a classic tiki syrup. Here they go in one at a time. The balance is mine: more of the lime, the grapefruit, the cinnamon and the falernum, so it's brighter and fresher. And I make the falernum myself (a sweet syrup of lime, cloves and rum that goes into many tiki drinks), as a nod to all the years he spent asking what was in things: with a bought bottle, you'd have to take the maker's word for it. It's shaken, then poured into a tall Zombie glass full of crushed ice, and topped with mint. It's a big drink and a strong one, made to be taken slowly.

One more thing from Berry's story. On his own, he got "rum and fruit juice". When he went in with Ted Haigh, a loud, sociable fellow historian whom one writer called Berry's opposite, he left with a recipe. "The first Don the Beachcomber recipes I got were because of Ted," Berry said. So take the question you've carried longest, and ask it out loud to the person you know who's least like you, the one who'd ask a stranger anything. Ask before you're sure it's a good question. You may get there years sooner, and on the day it all falls into place, you won't be the only one who's glad.
